title: The chain rule
story:
The chain rule is one line of calculus: the derivative of a composition is the product of the derivatives along it. Every reader of this track has met it. What makes it the engine of everything downstream is not the rule but the direction you apply it in, and that is a computational question rather than a mathematical one.

Consider the shape of the problem. A network's loss is a single number reached through a long composition, and it depends on millions of parameters. You want the derivative of that one number with respect to each of them. The chain rule can be accumulated from the inputs forwards or from the output backwards, and mathematically the answer is identical. Computationally they are wildly different, because of what a single sweep yields. Forward accumulation gives the derivatives of every output with respect to one input. Reverse accumulation gives the derivative of one output with respect to every input. So the efficient direction depends entirely on the ratio of inputs to outputs — and the cost of a reverse sweep is essentially the cost of the forward evaluation.

Look at that against the shape above. Millions of parameters, one scalar loss. Forward mode would need one sweep per parameter; reverse mode needs one sweep in total. That ratio is the entire reason training a large network is possible at all, and it is why the algorithm is a statement about accounting rather than about neural networks.

Which is also why the history is more crowded than the standard telling. Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams described the procedure in Nature in 1986 — it repeatedly adjusts the weights so as to minimise a measure of the difference between the actual output vector and the desired one, and the hidden units come to represent important features of the task domain, which is the ability to create useful new features that distinguishes it from earlier methods like the perceptron-convergence procedure. That paper deserves its fame. It is not, however, where the method comes from.

The reverse mode was published earlier and elsewhere. Linnainmaa's master's thesis at the University of Helsinki in 1970, with an English version in 1976, is often cited as its first published description — written about accumulated rounding error, with no reference to neural networks at all. Werbos formalised it in a doctoral thesis at Harvard in 1974, Beyond Regression, which did contain some preliminary network-specific discussion. Within the machine learning community it was then reinvented several times, including by Parker in 1985, before 1986 made it famous. The honest summary is that the mathematics arrived from numerical analysis, the application to networks arrived separately, and the fame arrived last.

problem.name: Reverse mode accumulation
problem.shape: A quantity depends on many parameters through a long composition of functions, and you need its derivative with respect to all of them.
tell: the loss is one number and the parameters are numerous
the dependency runs through many composed stages
a gradient is being estimated by perturbing parameters one at a time
memory rather than arithmetic is the binding constraint on depth
problem.move: Count the inputs and the outputs before choosing a direction. Accumulate backwards when there are many inputs and few outputs, which is the case for any scalar loss over parameters, and forwards when the ratio is reversed. Keep the intermediate values from the forward pass, and recompute rather than store them when memory is the constraint.
problem.invariant: Both directions compute the same derivatives. Reverse accumulation yields one output's derivative with respect to every input per sweep, forward accumulation yields every output's derivative with respect to one input, and the cost of a reverse sweep is essentially the cost of the forward evaluation.
problem.breaks: The advantage is entirely a function of the ratio. With one input and many outputs the reverse direction is the expensive one, requiring a sweep per output — so backpropagation is not a better algorithm than forward accumulation, it is the correct one for a particular shape that machine learning happens to have.

cost.time: one backward sweep, at roughly the cost of one forward evaluation, against one sweep per parameter for the alternative
cost.space: the intermediate values of the forward pass must be retained, so memory grows with the depth of the composition rather than with the parameter count
cost.beats: estimating each derivative by perturbing its parameter and re-evaluating, which costs a full evaluation per parameter and introduces approximation error on top

worked.problem: Why are derivatives accumulated backwards through a network rather than forwards, and what would the other direction cost?
worked.reasoning:
Because of the shape of the problem: many inputs, one output. The direction of accumulation decides the cost, and only one of the two directions is affordable here.

The chain rule itself says nothing about direction. The derivative of a composition is the product of the derivatives along the chain, and you may multiply that product together starting from either end; the answer is the same. What differs is what a single pass buys you.

Accumulate forwards, from the inputs, and one sweep gives you the derivatives of every output with respect to one input. If you have a million parameters, you need a million sweeps to get a million partial derivatives.

Accumulate backwards, from the output, and one sweep gives you the derivative of one output with respect to every input. One sweep, all million partial derivatives. And the cost of that backward sweep is essentially the cost of the forward evaluation — not the cost of a million of them.

So for a network the choice is not close. There are millions of parameters and exactly one scalar loss, which is the most favourable possible ratio for reverse accumulation. Forward mode would multiply the cost of training by the number of parameters, which is the difference between a model that trains overnight and one that does not train in a human lifetime.

The symmetry is worth stating because it stops this being a rule to memorise: forward mode is the right choice when the ratio is reversed. One input, many outputs — a sensitivity analysis with respect to a single quantity — and forward accumulation gets everything in one pass while reverse would need one sweep per output.

The price of the backward direction is memory. The backward sweep needs the intermediate values computed on the way forward, so they must be kept rather than discarded, and the memory required grows with the depth of the composition. That is the trade underneath activation checkpointing and every related technique: recompute intermediates to avoid storing them, spending time to buy space.

And this is why the algorithm is really a statement about accounting rather than about neural networks — which is consistent with the history, where the reverse mode was published in numerical analysis, in a thesis about accumulated rounding error, with no reference to networks at all.

problem.practice: Take a small composed function with three parameters and one output. Compute the gradient by hand both ways — forwards from each parameter, then backwards once from the output — and count the multiplications each direction required. Then work out what those two counts become at a million parameters.

beats.broke: A loss depends on its parameters only through a long composition of functions, and improving any one parameter requires knowing how the final number responds to a change in it.
beats.fix: Apply the chain rule in the direction that suits the shape. Accumulating from the output backwards gives the derivative of one number with respect to every parameter in a single sweep, at roughly the cost of one forward evaluation.
beats.cost: The backward sweep needs the intermediate values from the forward one, so they must be retained and memory grows with the depth of the composition rather than with the number of parameters.

interview.q: Why are derivatives accumulated backwards through a network rather than forwards, and what would the other direction cost?
interview.trap: Treating the backward direction as inherently superior. It is correct for many inputs and few outputs; invert that ratio and forward accumulation is the cheap one, which is why this is a statement about accounting rather than about neural networks.
interview.answer:
Because of the shape of the problem — many inputs and one output — and because the direction of accumulation decides the cost.

The chain rule is silent about direction. The derivative of a composition is the product of the derivatives along it, and that product can be multiplied together from either end for the same answer. What differs is what a single pass yields.

Forward accumulation gives the derivatives of every output with respect to one input. With a million parameters, that means a million sweeps for a million partial derivatives. Reverse accumulation gives the derivative of one output with respect to every input — one sweep for all of them — and the cost of that sweep is essentially the cost of the forward evaluation rather than a million times it.

For training a network the ratio could not be more favourable to reverse mode: millions of parameters and exactly one scalar loss. Forward mode would multiply the cost of training by the number of parameters, which is the difference between a model that trains overnight and one that never finishes.

I would state the symmetry too, because it stops this being a memorised rule. When the ratio is inverted — one input, many outputs, as in a sensitivity analysis with respect to a single quantity — forward mode is correct and gets everything in one pass while reverse would need a sweep per output. The algorithm is a statement about accounting, not about neural networks.

The price of going backwards is memory. The backward sweep needs the intermediate values from the forward pass, so they have to be retained rather than discarded, and the requirement grows with the depth of the composition. That trade is what activation checkpointing manages: recompute intermediates instead of storing them, spending time to buy space.
